digest.intro: A chokepoint seized, a pact signed, and the world's hidden layers made visible.

items.title: Houthis seize Perim Island — the other Red Sea chokepoint
items.blurb: Perim Island bisects the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gate between Asia and Europe, and the Houthis now control it — a move that matters more because Saudi Arabia has been rerouting oil through the Red Sea since the Strait of Hormuz closed. The BBC's Nawal Al-Maghafi adds the important nuance: Iran built the Houthis' missile and drone capacity over years, but doesn't script every decision — this is an indigenous strategic choice as much as a proxy action.

items.title: Bankruptcy as AI data acquisition vehicle
items.blurb: Google won the auction for Spirit Airlines' operational data in bankruptcy proceedings — but Springshot, whose platform ran Spirit's entire tech stack through the final flight, says a substantial portion of what's being sold is actually their IP, not Spirit's. The sale agreement uses definitions so vague ('productivity and collaboration data,' 'core business systems data') that no one can tell whose property is being transferred — and Springshot argues the court should pause the sale until a forensic audit draws the line.

items.title: The NASA algorithm that makes ancient paintings visible again
items.blurb: Decorrelation stretch — originally developed at JPL to pull more information from satellite imagery by amplifying subtle spectral differences — turned out to be exactly what archaeologists needed to recover faded rock art and lost paintings. A hobbyist named Jon Harman, whose side interest in rock art happened to collide with his image-processing background, built the tool that brought back 200 invisible paintings from the walls of Angkor Wat, rediscovered between 2010 and 2012. The same algorithm that reads Mars is reading the Pleistocene.

items.title: Where construction automation actually succeeded — and why almost everywhere else it failed
items.blurb: Brian Potter fed thousands of back-issues of construction trade journals into AI trawlers going back to 1853 and found a stark pattern: successful automation in construction falls into exactly two categories — tasks moved off-site into factory conditions, and on-site tasks so repetitive a machine can do them in a straight line. Direct labor is still ~50% of a U.S. home's cost versus 6-8% for a car, and that gap has resisted 170 years of attempts. The insight is immediately portable to digital fabrication: the question isn't whether you can automate a step, it's whether you can make the conditions factory-like enough for automation to hold.

items.title: What happens when you redesign the inside of a 3D printer nozzle
items.blurb: Thomas Sanladerer SLS-printed nozzles with exotic internal geometries — triple-split material paths, various intrusions to maximize melt contact area — then tested them on a Prusa Core One with a custom pressure rig to find where each design buckles under high flow. The 'Fuge' design won, though it's printed in MS1 tool steel, which is not ideal nozzle material; the more interesting result is that the pressure-characterization methodology itself is now in the open, giving anyone a replicable way to benchmark nozzle geometry.

items.title: CNC Kitchen: head-to-head 3D scanner shootout
items.blurb: Stefan Geisler is the most methodical tester in the maker space — he builds fixtures, runs controlled comparisons, and shows his numbers rather than vibes. A head-to-head scanner comparison from him means actual resolution and accuracy data under real conditions, which is exactly what you need before dropping money on capture hardware for a physical/digital pipeline.

items.title: The 1816 children's book that taught death through paper flaps
items.blurb: A Philadelphia flap book from 1816 let children manipulate paper tabs to transform Adam into Eve into a mermaid, a lion into a griffin into an eagle — and then, inevitably, into a skeleton — while a disclaimer on the first page clarified that mermaids and griffins are fictional but death is not. The object is a state machine disguised as a toy, and it's descended from a single-sheet pamphlet from the English Civil War whose figures suspiciously resemble Charles I. The physical/digital transformation problem, solved in paper, 200 years before WebGL.

facts.fact: Angkor Wat contains approximately 200 paintings that were invisible to the naked eye and were only discovered between 2010 and 2012 using a satellite image-processing algorithm originally developed by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Direct labor accounts for roughly 50% of the cost of building a U.S. single-family home, compared to just 6–8% for manufacturing a car — a gap that has persisted despite 170 years of automation attempts dating back to an 1853 plastering machine.

Saudi Arabia has been routing oil exports through the Red Sea rather than the Strait of Hormuz since the Strait was effectively closed by the U.S.-Israel war with Iran — making the Houthis' seizure of Perim Island, which divides the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a direct threat to Saudi export capacity.

Springshot, the startup whose platform powered Spirit Airlines' entire technology stack through its final flight, says it received no notice before Google won the bankruptcy auction for Spirit's data — and the sale agreement's definitions are broad enough to potentially transfer Springshot's own IP.

The 1816 flap book 'Metamorphosis' is descended from a single-sheet Civil War pamphlet first printed in 1650 whose figures bear a suspicious resemblance to Charles I — making it possibly a political document disguised as a children's toy for nearly four centuries.

art_picks.title: Leviathan
art_picks.creator: Lucien Castaing-Taylor & Véréna Paravel
art_picks.why: A fishing trawler rendered as pure sensory system — cameras lashed to nets, hooks, and hulls produce something genuinely alien, a document of labor and ocean that sits exactly at the edge where physical reality becomes abstract image. No narration, no thesis; just the feedback loop of industrial violence and beauty.

art_picks.title: Vera Molnár — Retrospective
art_picks.creator: Vera Molnár
art_picks.why: The godmother of generative art, who spent decades hand-simulating algorithms before computers existed to run them — her entire practice is a meditation on rule, deviation, and the moment a system becomes expressive. For anyone building generative 3D, this is the lineage.

art_picks.title: Vis
art_picks.creator: Elori Saxl
art_picks.why: Saxl built synthesis instruments from field recordings of water and wind, then composed music indistinguishable from natural phenomena — the album functions like a feedback system between technology and environment. It rewards the kind of attention that looks for the hidden structure underneath a surface.

events.name: Camille Henrot: Dogs
events.venue: Doris C. Freedman Plaza, Central Park (5th Ave & 60th St)
events.why: Henrot's dog sculptures read as deceptively domestic objects that are actually dense symbol systems — she uses the domesticated animal as a lens on co-dependence, care, and the rituals of everyday life; free, public, and worth catching while the September light holds.

events.name: Taryn Simon | Father Country I Do Love You — Opening
events.venue: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, 1071 5th Ave, Manhattan
events.why: Simon fills the entire Wright rotunda — for the first time with a photography-based artist — with 42 interconnected works tracing an unnamed federal agent's life across Cold War geographies, folding personal family history and state power into one interactive labyrinth: exactly the kind of hidden-system narrative that rewards slow looking.

events.name: MESS IS LORE Vol. 7 at Light & Sound Design
events.venue: Light & Sound Design (Brooklyn — exact address on site)
events.why: Light & Sound Design runs one of Brooklyn's most obsessively curated sound spaces — vintage Klipschorn system, private loft, serious listening culture — the kind of venue built around the idea that acoustic design is itself an artistic act.

events.name: Spring/Break Art Show
events.venue: TBA (announced closer to date — historically in Midtown Manhattan)
events.why: The anti-Armory fair: artist-curated, conceptually driven, uses found spaces — historically a better place to stumble onto genuinely strange work than any of the polished booths across town, and running the same week as the Armory makes the contrast instructive.

events.name: The Armory Show 2026
events.why: 230+ galleries from 30+ countries, with the curated Focus and Platform sections built around Caribbean-led curatorial narratives — more geographically specific and less Eurocentric than prior editions, and worth the walk for the Presents section spotlighting galleries under 12 years old.
